Environmental Conditions and Macrophytes of Karst Ponds Igor Zelnik*, Mateja Potisek, Alenka Gaberščik Department of Biology, Biotechnical Faculty, University of Ljubljana, Večna pot 111, 1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia Received: 19 December 2011 Accepted: 13 June 2012 Abstract Man-made karst ponds are the only surface water bodies in the Karst region (SW Slovenia, NE Italy) and support variable biotic communities, depending on ecological parameters and human activities. The aim of our study was to establish the relationship between environmental conditions (land-use of the catchment, vegetation of the banktop zone, morphological properties of the ponds, water quality parameters, the presence of fish) and aquatic macrophyte species composition and abundance. The survey of 28 ponds was performed in the peak vegetation period in 2009. The most abundant emergent macrophytes found were Typha latifolia, Alisma plantago-aquatica, Eleocharis palustris agg., and Alisma lanceolatum, while the most common hydrophytes were Lemna minor, Chara spp., Nymphaea alba, and Potamogeton natans. About 15% of all species found in ponds are included in the “Red” list of endangered plant species of Slovenia. The presence of fish, water transparency, pH, land-use of the pond catchment and quality of shore substrate were detected as the most influential factors determining aquatic macrophyte communities. Keywords: Karst, pond, environmental parameter, floristic composition Introduction Ponds are small lentic ecosystems that permanently or temporarily hold water [1]. They are shallow and their size ranges from a few square metres to several hectares. They can be natural or man-made. Their number is much higher than that of large lakes, which constitute a small percentage of the total number of lakes [2]. Despite this, studies of lentic ecosystems have concentrated mainly on moderately large lakes [2]. Ponds differ functionally from larger lakes [3], since their littoral structure and its productivity dominates the ecosystem [2]. Despite their small size they contain a significant part of aquatic biodiversity on the landscape scale [4, 5]. Humans have created millions of ponds for multiple purposes [2], but today they serve as refugia for a variety of freshwater biota [5] and are, as such, an irreplaceable type of habitat [6-8]. The biotic communities that develop in ponds depend on environmental conditions and human activity. Several studies document clear associations between the communities and a variety of environmental gradients, such as hydro-period [9, 10], surface area [11], and water properties like water transparency, nutrient availability, and pH [12-14]. Compared to rivers and lakes, ponds exhibit greater environmental and, consequently, biotic amplitudes [15]. Macrophytes are important components of aquatic ecosystems (including ponds), affecting their function through energy flow, nutrient cycling, sedimentation processes, and habitat provision [16, 17]. Their presence and abundance reflect the quality of the ecosystem as a whole. Aquatic macrophytes not only are affected by water quality, but they also affect water quality and provide food and refugia for aquatic invertebrates and fish [11, 18, 19]. Their growth is controlled by a variety of factors, namely water quality, water depth, water movement, substrate characteristics, and biotic interactions [20, 21]. Therefore, a survey of aquatic macrophytes is important from the point of 1912 Zelnik I., et al. view of plant species diversity, as well as of factors explaining the diversity of other groups (e.g. macro-invertebrates, periphyton) [22] and as indicators of water and habitat quality [e.g. 23-28]. Deterioration of the physical environment and eutrophication of water bodies result in changes in macrophyte distribution, a decline in aquatic macrophyte species richness, and a greater abundance of more resistant species [29]. Karst ponds are of human origin, presenting an outstanding natural and cultural heritage [30]. Following mass regulation of rivers and streams all over Europe, man-made systems have become a substitute habitat for numerous organisms [6]. This is the case in the karst ponds, which provide an important network of water-bodies in the Karst Region. The fact, that they are the only surface water-bodies on the Karst Plateau [31] makes them even more important. The aims of our study were to examine the habitat characteristics and/or ecological conditions in karst ponds, as well as surveying the presence and abundance of aquatic macrophyte species. We also aimed to establish the relations between habitat characteristics and aquatic macrophyte species composition. The specific questions addressed were: • Which environmental conditions significantly influence aquatic macrophyte species composition in karst ponds? • How much of the variation of aquatic macrophyte species composition is explained by considered environmental conditions and how do they affect macrophytes species richness? Materials and Methods Study Area Twenty-eight karst ponds were investigated in the Karst region in SW Slovenia. The ponds are distributed on the Karst Plateau along the border with Italy (from 13°38’08” E, 45°50’43” N to 13°59’36” E, 45°39’54” N) (Table 1). The climate is sub-Mediterranean, annual precipitation is 1,500 mm [32] (about two-fold higher than evapotranspiration). The largest amount of precipitation occurs in November, and the least in the peak of the vegetation period in July [32]. The mean annual temperature is 11°C [33]. The altitude ranges from 195 to 420 m a.s.l. Aquatic Macrophyte Survey The abundance of aquatic macrophytes was evaluated using a 5-degree estimation scale [34]: 1 = very rare 2 = infrequent 3 = common 4 = frequent 5 = abundant, predominant The whole pond was a sampling unit. Plants were identified using the following keys: Martinčič et al. [35] and Preston [36]. Plants whose reproductive organs were not present at the time of sampling are listed by genus (e.g. Bidens, Epilobium, Sparganium). The survey was performed in July and August in 2009. The nomenclature of ferns and flowering plants follows Martinčič et al. [35]. The definition of aquatic macrophytes is in accordance with Hutchinson [37] and Wetzel [2], therefore woody species and other non-hygrophilous species were excluded from analyses. Plant species richness in the ponds was calculated as species number (N) per surface area and/or approximate volume of the studied water bodies.

Independent environmental variables were tested for their significance in shaping aquatic macrophyte species composition. These variables can be classified into three groups [38]: quantitative variables, semiquantitative estimates, and categorical variables. Quantitative variables include morphometric parameters of the specific pond (length, width or diameter (m), surface (m²), depth (m), approximate volume (m³), surface:depth ratio (S/d)), and water quality parameters (pH, temperature (T), conductivity (EC), O₂ concentration, O₂ saturation, transparency, chlorophyll-a). Semiquantitative estimates include habitat characteristics (land-use of the catchment, bottom substrate, shore substrate, type of vegetation in banktop zone, width of woody and/or wetland banktop zone). Categorical variables include data about the presence/absence of: fish, filamentous algae, slime, woody species in the pond. Water samples were taken from each pond in August 2009. The majority of the water quality parameters (pH, O₂ concentration, O₂ saturation, T and EC of water) were measured in situ using the portable multi-meter PCD 650 (Eutech Instruments, Singapore). Water transparency and concentration of chlorophyll-a were analyzed spectrophotometrically in the laboratory on the same day. Habitat characteristics were assessed as semiquantitative estimates in a similar way as in many studies of aquatic ecosystems [39-41]. The estimated gradients were as follows: (1) land-use of the pond catchment, according to decreasing human influence (1 = settlement or arable land/vineyard or road, 2 = mixed arable land and grassland, 3 = grassland, 4 = mixed grassland and forest, 5 = forest) (2) the type and/or structure of the shore substrate, according to decreasing coarseness of the substrate (1 = concrete, 2 = stone-wall, 3 = stones and stone-wall, 4 = stones, 5 = loam and clay) (3) of the bottom (1 = concrete, 2 = stones and concrete, 3 = stones, 4 = stones and loam, 5 = loam and clay) (4) width of the littoral zone (1 = <1 m, 2 = 1-5 m, 3 = >5 m) (5) vegetation of the banktop zone, according to decreasing human influence (1 = absent, 2 = ruderals, 3 = perennial herbs and grasses, 4 = pioneer woody species (Salix sp., Populus sp.), 5 = climax species of trees and shrubs). Statistical Analyses Detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) was used for exploratory data analysis. The eigenvalue for the first DCA axis was greater than 0.4 and indicated strong unimodality [42], therefore canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) was chosen. Relationships between site conditions and vegetation were analyzed using direct gradient analysis (CCA). Separate CCAs for each environmental variable were performed to test the significance of its influence and the explanation of species composition variation. Forward selection of explanatory variables was used to provide a ranking of the relative importance of the specific variables and to avoid co-linearity [43]. We used the unrestricted Monte Carlo test with 999 permutations to test the statistical significance of the variables and canonical axes. Another CCA was done with a subset of selected variables only (p<0.1), and the proportions of variance explained by these variables were calculated. Some of the variables were not normally distributed so the data were log transformed. Ordination of the ponds according to the most important environmental parameters was made using CCA. The whole set of analyses was performed using CANOCO 4.5 [44]. Differences in environmental parameters between ponds with and without macrophytes were tested for significance using t-test. Species richness was correlated with environmental parameters using Spearman coefficient in SPSS version 17. Results Aquatic Macrophyte Survey Different growth forms of plants were found: submerged hydrophytes, floating hydrophytes, helophytes, marsh species, and flood-meadow species (Table 3). The most abundant aquatic macrophyte species found in karst ponds were: Typha latifolia, Lemna minor, Alisma plantago-aquatica, Eleocharis palustris, Chara spp., Alisma lanceolatum, and Potamogeton natans. Species from the Red List of Slovenia [45] are relatively numerous, constituting 15% of the total of 50 plant species recorded in ponds. Floristically Defined Types of Karst Ponds Leaving aside the smaller group of ponds that contained no aquatic macrophytes, the ordination plot based on results of preliminary DCA showed clustering of the ponds according to floristic composition. Two groups of ponds that were ecologically sound were delineated – a group of seven less similar species-poorer, mostly walled ponds, and the larger group of 15 species-richer ponds with loamy shores. The group of walled ponds was species-poorer and characterized by the presence of different pond-weeds (Potamogeton crispus, P. nodosus, P. natans, P. trichoides) and a higher proportion of other submerged and/or floating hydrophytes, which constitute half of the species. The group of relatively shallow ponds was characterized by a significantly higher total number of plant taxa, with Typha latifolia, Alisma lanceolata, Eleocharis palustris agg., Juncus inflexus, J. effusus, and other emergent macrophytes and marsh species. Emergent species constitute a quarter of all species, hydrophytes only 12%, and marsh species were most common, constituting 36% of the plant taxa. Environmental Conditions and Gradients A preliminary DCA revealed a first gradient length of 6.49 SD, which indicates strong unimodality, so CCA was chosen. Separate CCAs for each environmental variable revealed that some of the variables influence floristic composition significantly: fish presence, water transparency, pH, land-use of the catchment, and shore substrate. Analysis with forward selection provided a ranking of the relative importance of the specific significant variables (Table 4). The presence of fish, water transparency, pH, land-use of the catchment area of the pond, and shore substrate were revealed to be the most influential factors determining aquatic macrophyte communities, explaining species variation significantly. The differences were most significant in the case of shore substrate (p < 0.05), which was concrete, or a stone wall in the first case and mostly loamy, or a mixture of stones and loam, in the latter. Discussion Floristic Gradients and Environmental Parameters The variation of floristic composition is best explained by the following environmental variables: fish presence/absence, water transparency, pH, land-use of the catchment of the pond, and substrate of the shore. Mentioned parameters explained 32% of the variance in plant species composition that was similar to the results obtained for aquatic macrophytes in karstic watercourses in western Slovenia [46], where a similar set of the studied variables explain 28% of the variation. Capers et al. [13] obtained a similar result (27%), while the results by McElarney et al. [47] revealed higher value (56%). The unexplained variation may also be explained by sampling errors, other non-measured parameters, and by the fact that the species-specific recruitment from the soil seed bank and its persistence has a significant impact on the structure and maintenance of the plant-species diversity in wet habitats [48]. Floristic composition was most strongly correlated by fish-presence (7.9% of total variance was explained by this parameter) which, in contrast, had no influence on species richness or the presence of Red List species. A strong role of fish was also found in the study of peri-urban eutrophic ponds by De Backer et al. [14]. Water transparency explained 6.6% of species variance, in accordance with studies showing the importance of submerged macrophytes in maintaining the clear-water state [14, 49, 50]. The amount of phytoplankton, measured as the concentration of chlorophyll-a, was very variable and did not significantly affect plant species composition or abundance, as was shown by Bakker et al. [51]. The number of plant taxa found in 28 karst ponds was 50, which was high compared to the 53 plant taxa found in 9 streams flowing through the agricultural landscape of Eastern Slovenia, and were considered to support rich aquatic macrophyte communities [52]. The percentage of Red List species was relatively high (15%) and similar to results published by Chappuis et al. [53]. Table 4. Canonical Correspondence analysis statistics of 22 karstic ponds. CCA with these five variables (Table 4) was performed, allowing the distribution of the ponds according to floristic composition along the most important environmental gradients to be shown in an ordination diagram (Fig. 1). Ponds with prevailing hydrophytes are distributed on the upper-right side of the diagram in the direction of fish presence (and transparency), which indicates oxic conditions throughout the year in the permanent water phase. Hypoxic conditions normally occur in ponds with a strong input of allochthonous leaf litter in autumn. Species-rich ponds with abundant emergent and marsh species are distributed in the lower-left part of the diagram in the direction of finer shore substrate, enabling the growth of the mentioned species. Arrows representing water transparency and land-use indicate relative correlation that was expected, since the higher proportion of forest or permanent grassland in the catchment area of a pond would result in clearer water. Species number was significantly correlated with surface/depth ratio, shore substrate, surface area of the pond and width of littoral zone (Table 5). The ponds with loamy shores and/or wider littoral zone were not only richer in total species number, but also harboured more Red list species, which were also more abundant. Environmental Factors in Different Pond Types The main differences in environmental conditions between ponds without macrophytes and those with more or less abundant macrophytes, are the type of shore-substrate (p = 0.014) and of bottom-substrate (p = 0.099), as well as the pH of the water (p = 0.078). The mean recorded pH value in ponds without macrophytes was 7.2, while in ponds with plants it was 6.7. The differences were most significant in the case of shore substrate (p < 0.05), which was concrete, or a stone wall in the first case and mostly loamy, or a mixture of stones and loam, in the latter. **p < 0.01, * = p < 0.05, n.s. = not significant Some studies relate the ratio of submerged to emerged macrophyte species with the level of eutrophication [51]. In our study the abundance of helophytes prevailed over that of submerged species. This was not necessarily the consequence of nutrient availability since, in many case, this parameter does not function as a primary factor shaping the aquatic macrophyte community; other factors affecting ecological conditions, such as water depth and fluctuation, could be of greater importance [54]. However, if we take into account the aquatic macrophyte indicator values for ponds proposed by Sager and Lachavanne [27], the surveyed ponds were shown to host species indicating a mesotrophic as well as a mesotrophic to eutrophic state. Water pH was expected to have a significant influence on aquatic macrophyte assemblages, as indicated by a study of alpine ponds [12]. Land-use practices may affect pond characteristics [5, 13, 15, 55, 56], and these changes of the pond environment (e.g. water/sediment quality) may affect aquatic organisms, their species richness, and abundance. Dodson [56] also concluded that land-use was a good predictor of pond biodiversity. In our study, land-use of the catchment of the pond was not significantly correlated with species-richness, but with species composition. Differences in Environmental Factors between Pond Types As expected, the type of shore substrate provided the most significant difference between ponds with and without macrophytes. The semi-natural types of shore, with finely textured substrate (clay, silt and/or loam), were suitable sites (microhabitats) for emergent macrophytes, while in the case of concrete or stony shores, rooted aquatic macrophytes were scarce. The difference in pH between ponds with macrophytes and “empty” ponds also was evident (p = 0.078). The higher pH of the water in non-colonizd ponds could be due to the contribution of Ca-rich concrete and/or stony substrate. Species number did not correlate with depth, but was significantly correlated with size/depth ratio and surface. In the case of alpine lakes [12] depth did not affect biodiversity, while a significant influence of pond size on the aquatic macrophyte community was shown by Bagella et al. [57], who studied Mediterranean temporary ponds. They also established the important role of disturbances. The main disturbances in the ponds studied here are water level fluctuations, since the conditions of ponds in the Karst region depends directly on precipitation [30], which is unequally distributed over the year [32]. In many cases disturbances also could be the consequence of the land-use in the surroundings of the ponds, i.e. trampling, erosion, and invasive species [50]. In our survey invasive alien plant species were not detected in the ponds and were not abundant in the littoral zone. The most abundant species was the invasive tree species Robinia pseudacacia, which is widespread in the Karst region and is important from the point of nitrogen enrichment of ponds [58]. The ponds with more suitable measures (e.g. loamy shores, wider littoral zone) were not only richer in total species number, but also harbored more Red list species, which also were more abundant. To mitigate adverse effects on plant communities, Akasaka et al. [50] suggests that management should focus on the creation of buffer zones. Conclusions Understanding the environmental conditions that maintain high aquatic macrophyte species richness in karst ponds, together with the main disturbances threatening them, is crucial for the conservation of this important heritage. Land-use in the catchment area and the presence of fish-influenced plant species composition. Concrete shores and bottoms, as well as stony walls, prevented the development of complex aquatic macrophyte communities and the increase of species richness. We conclude that reinforcement of the shores with concrete is the main reason for species impoverishment in karst ponds. On the other hand, some species (Potamogeton crispus, P. nodosus) were found only in walled ponds and that contributes to gamma diversity. As was established for alpine lakes [12], karst ponds need a special approach due to the particular water regime in the Karst area. The present findings should be considered in restoration projects, in order to preserve diversity at all levels. Acknowledgements We thank Prof. Roger Pain for correction of the language. We also thank Dragan Abram for his technical assistance in the field and in the laboratory. We are grateful for critical comments and suggestions of the reviewer that helped to improve the quality of the paper.

Environmental Conditions and Macrophytes... 1913 Assessment of Environmental Conditions Parameters were recorded in the field, measured and/or calculated in the laboratory (Table 2). Independent environmental variables were tested for their significance in shaping aquatic macrophyte species composition. These variables can be classified into three groups [38]: quantitative variables, semiquantitative estimates, and categorical variables. Quantitative variables include morphometric parameters of the specific pond (length, width or diameter (m), surface (m²), depth (m), approximate volume (m³), surface:depth ratio (S/d)), and water quality parameters (pH, temperature (T), conductivity (EC), O₂ concentration, O₂ saturation, transparency, chlorophyll-a). Semiquantitative estimates include habitat characteristics (land-use of the catchment, bottom substrate, shore substrate, type of vegetation in banktop zone, width of woody and/or wetland banktop zone). Categorical variables include data about the presence/absence of: fish, filamentous algae, slime, woody species in the pond. Water samples were taken from each pond in August 2009. The majority of the water quality parameters (pH, O₂ concentration, O₂ saturation, T and EC of water) were measured in situ using the portable multi-meter PCD 650 (Eutech Instruments, Singapore). Water transparency and concentration of chlorophyll-a were analyzed spectrophotometrically in the laboratory on the same day. Habitat characteristics were assessed as semiquantitative estimates in a similar way as in many studies of aquatic ecosystems [39-41]. The estimated gradients were as follows: (1) land-use of the pond catchment, according to decreasing human influence (1 = settlement or arable land/vineyard or road, 2 = mixed arable land and grassland, 3 = grassland, 4 = mixed grassland and forest, 5 = forest) (2) the type and/or structure of the shore substrate, according to decreasing coarseness of the substrate (1 = concrete, 2 = stone-wall, 3 = stones and stone-wall, 4 = stones, 5 = loam and clay) (3) of the bottom (1 = concrete, 2 = stones and concrete, 3 = stones, 4 = stones and loam, 5 = loam and clay) (4) width of the littoral zone (1 = <1 m, 2 = 1-5 m, 3 = >5 m) (5) vegetation of the banktop zone, according to decreasing human influence (1 = absent, 2 = ruderals, 3 = perennial herbs and grasses, 4 = pioneer woody species (Salix sp., Populus sp.), 5 = climax species of trees and shrubs). Statistical Analyses Detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) was used for exploratory data analysis. The eigenvalue for the first DCA axis was greater than 0.4 and indicated strong unimodality [42], therefore canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) was chosen. Relationships between site conditions and vegetation were analyzed using direct gradient analysis (CCA). Separate CCAs for each environmental variable were performed to test the significance of its influence and the explanation of species composition variation. The resulting transformations removed both objections, and enabled the fitting of the linear regression lines of yield on area shown in Figure 1. The formula for each regression is: Total population: \( \log y = (2.4294 - .4001 \log x) \) Annual sport yield: \( \log y = (1.8692 - .3884 \log x) \) Annual commercial yield: \( \log y = (3.0355 - .3906 \log x) \) ![Graph showing annual yield of gamefish per acre of water surface for lakes from 30 to 50,000 acres in area](page_324_670_1207_1012.png) Figure 2. Calculated curves of the annual sport fishery (gamefish) yield in pounds per acre of water surface for lakes from 30 to 50,000 acres in area. [These curves are derived from the antilogarithms of the regression of annual sport yield on lake area shown in figure 1.] The standard error of estimate was calculated for each regression, and appears (dotted lines) for each regression line in Figure 1. It will be noted that all three measures of fish production show the same rate of decline with increasing size of lake. These data are given in Table II. No attempt has been made to extrapolate the yields for lakes outside the range of sizes available for each type of data. The annual yield of game fish is also shown in Figure 2 in such form that it may be conveniently and quickly estimated for lakes of any size from 30 to 50,000 acres in area. The most obvious characteristic of the yields is the rapid decline in production per acre as the lakes increase in size. The optimistic production estimates of most fishery experts are not borne out; but it is believed that this is owing largely to the fact that such opinions have been based on the production of very small ponds. For instance, the total population falls from 268.5 pounds in ponds of one acre to only 32.3 pounds in lakes of 200 acres. In the range of lakes for which total populations are available, i.e., 1 to 200 acres, the annual yield of sport fish varies from 74.0 to 9.46 pounds per acre, or 27.6 to 29.3 per cent of the total population estimate. As the total populations include fish of all sizes, as well as forage and rough fishes not contained in the gamefish catch, it is obvious that the sportsmen annually harvest a very appreciable proportion of the available gamefish of legal size. In many of the lakes analyzed, even the surprisingly low yields shown could not be sustained in the face of intensive fishing. The commercial catch per acre is much higher than the sport catch in lakes of 10,000 to 50,000 acres. Thus, at 50,000 acres, the sport catch was only 1.11 pounds per acre compared with a commercial catch of 15.85 pounds. This is owing to several causes. First, sport fisheries are carried on in all lakes, while commercial fisheries are confined to selected lakes of higher than average productivity. Second, the commercial fisheries take many rough fishes and pelagic fishes such as lake herring which are not taken by sportsmen. Third, the commercial fisheries usually impose higher fishing intensities. The yield per acre of lake is probably correlated with the relative area of fertile shallow water, which is generally much less in proportion to total area in the larger lakes than in the smaller ones, as indicated by the difference in length of shoreline. Thus, a circular lake of 503 acres has a shoreline of 3.14 miles, or 0.00624 miles per acre, while one of 50,200 acres has a shoreline of only 31.42 miles, or 0.000626 miles per acre, or about one-tenth as much shoreline per acre. Obviously, the shallow, fertile areas usually are relatively much less extensive in the larger lakes. There are various reasons for variation in the yield of lakes of similar size. Some of these differences are related to the physical and chemical conditions of the lake itself, such as depth, temperature, heat budget, and the quantities of various nutrient materials available. Others relate to the populations of fish and other organisms present. Even in lakes which are comparable both physically and chemically, the yield may differ considerably because of a difference in the species present. Making allowances for physical and chemical characteristics, and for annual variations in climatic conditions, the yield of a lake depends in large measure on the natural balance of the populations within the lake. Only occasionally will a lake be producing at its maximum potential capacity. As an illustration, I have drawn upon data given by Foerster (1944) and by Ricker (1937) for Cultus Lake, British Columbia. Foerster gives the number and weight of the young sockeye salmon migrating out of Cultus Lake each year during a 12-year period. (See Table III.) The balance that had obtained during the first nine years of this period was upset during the last three by the extensive removal of species preying on and competing with the sockeye. 36 COPEIA 1946, No. 1 April 30 The data of Table III and the curves in Figure 3 show some interesting relationships. At low levels of abundance (under one million) the relation between the number of sockeye and their total weight appears to be linear. This indicates that at these levels the young sockeye were not competing with one another for food, so that the size of the individuals depended on conditions other than competition. Because, then, of natural limits to the growth potential of the individual, the maximum productivity of the lake was not reached with these small populations (Area A, Figure 3). In the absence of competition, increasing size of population was accompanied by increasing total weight of fish produced. At what point competition began to be a limiting factor is not shown by the data, but at higher levels of abundance (in 1933 and 1929) the growth rate of the individual sockeye was greatly diminished. The maximum productivity can be reached, therefore, only when sockeye are neither too few nor too numerous. A parallel situation occurs in many lakes in which predators are too scarce to keep down the abundance of perch, resulting in populations of stunted perch. Curve 2 shows the line of approximate maximum production under natural conditions. Curve 3 shows the indicated production for the three years in which the predators and competing species were suppressed. Area A shows the weight lost from the maximum natural production caused chiefly by a population insufficient to utilize the total food supply. Area B shows the weight lost from the maximum natural production when too large a population is present. The suggested cause is the larger amount of food used to sustain life without growth and actual impairment of the food supply owing to the large numbers of fish per unit area.] These curves of production in natural lakes are at present the only guide for predicting the fish production in proposed reservoirs. A reservoir usually differs in certain important features from a natural lake. It is more subject to frequent and severe fluctuations in water level. It is more apt to have the bottom covered with layers of silt. The deep water usually is confined to one end, causing unnatural temperature stratifications. All of these features tend to make the reservoir less productive than the natural lake. Because of the large quantities of organic matter present when first flooded, reservoirs may show a high initial productivity which will be reduced within a short space of years when they have begun to approach as close to a state of equilibrium as a reservoir is likely to attain. Because the productive capacity of a reservoir must be estimated over a long period of years rather than in the short period immediately following construction when production may be high, it follows that the estimate of yield, based on the analysis of yields of natural lakes, will tend to be too high rather than too low. Nevertheless, it seems desirable that pending detailed studies, these data be used to estimate the productivity of proposed reservoirs. How much adjustment in predicted yield needs to be made for the limiting factors discussed above will remain a matter of opinion until adequate studies of these problems have been made. Habitat characteristics and odonate diversity in mountain ponds of central Italy GIANMARIA CARCHINIa·*, ANGELO GIUSEPPE SOLIMINIb and ANTONIO RUGGIEROa a Dipartimento di Biologia, Università Tor Vergata, Roma, Italy b European Commission Joint Research Centre, Institute for Environment and Sustainability, Inland and Marine Waters Unit, Ispra, Italy ABSTRACT 1. In central Italy mountain ponds represent an important habitat for the conservation of dragonflies; however, human disturbance of these fragile environments is threatening the stability of their biodiversity. 2. Thirty-one ponds, ranging in altitude from 1014 to 2004 m, were qualitatively sampled for odonate larvae twice during 1998. On each occasion a range of physical, chemical and biotic habitat variables were also measured. 3. The mountain ponds sampled had fewer species of Odonata than lowland ponds, and there was a large presence of pioneer species. 4. Multiple regression analysis showed that the number of odonate species was positively affected by the amount of macrophyte coverage of the pond surface and negatively affected by increasing ammonium concentration. 5. A Canonical Correspondence Analysis revealed that species number decreased with altitude, chlorophyll a and phosphorus concentrations. The presence/absence of each odonate species was weakly related to the habitat variables. 6. The intensive use of ponds for livestock watering results in damage to the peripheral vegetation, which tends to cause high turbidity and lower macrophyte coverage of the pond water. The inevitable outcome in these situations is a reduction of the odonate diversity. KEY WORDS: dragonfly; lentic species; conservation; aquatic vegetation; mountain habitat; land use INTRODUCTION The Odonata are one of the most important animal taxa of freshwater habitats, especially in ponds, where they can often be the top predators. Unfortunately, due to human modification of habitat structure and the drying up of smaller freshwater environments, there is a major threat to the number of odonate species as *Correspondence to: Prof. G. Carchini, Dipartimento di Biologia, Università Tor Vergata, I-00133, Roma, Italy. E-mail: carchini@uniroma2.it well as many other pond-inhabiting taxa. This has been shown to be particularly true in developed countries, with reductions of suitable biotopes of more than 50% in the last century (see a review in Corbet (1999, 565–566)). As a consequence, odonate populations in Europe as a whole are in decline (Wildermuth, 1994); it has been shown that 22 species out of ca. 130 have declining populations or restricted distributions (Sahlén et al., 2004). In Italy, out of a total of 88 species two are considered already extinct, and eight, including three subspecies, are considered seriously endangered (Utzeri, 1994). In addition, Odonata have been considered as biological indicators for both running and still waters (Schmidt, 1985; Corbet, 1993; Chovanec and Raab, 1997; Chovanec, 2000, Chovanec and Waringer, 2001, Chovanec et al., 2004). More specifically, the Odonata have been chosen as indicator taxa in systems for evaluating the environmental value of ponds (Godreau et al. 1999; Briers and Biggs, 2003). Therefore, there is a requirement for a better understanding of the relationship between odonate species and their habitats, which has been shown to differ between different topographical and geographical regions (Sahlén and Ekestubbe, 2001). The aim of this study was to obtain more information about habitat–odonate relationships in mountain ponds and to compare this information with that of a previously studied set of ponds in a well-preserved coastal plain in central Italy (Carchini et al., 2003). Owing to calcareous geology, throughout the mountain range of central Italy, surface waters tend to be scarce. The ponds are generally small and have been either preserved or created mainly for livestock watering. During the last decade, several nature reserves have been established in mountainous areas, but watering is still permitted. These ponds often represent the only still waters available for freshwater biota and the human pressures on these habitats might be in conflict with the conservation of their biodiversity. Regarding the Odonata, in central Italy (and the entire peninsular part of Italy) the distribution of some species is restricted to high altitudes, so these mountain ponds can represent key habitats for their conservation. METHODS Thirty-one naturally occurring or artificial ponds were sampled. These ponds were, presumed permanent, situated at altitudes higher than 1000 m in an area of the Apennines in central Italy with geographical limits of: 42° 00′ 00″ N, 42° 46′ 22″ N, 13° 05′ 00″ E and 13° 42′ 20″ E. For each pond, geographic location, altitude, area and forest percentage in a surrounding circle of 1000 m radius were assessed by maps and aerial photographs at 1/2000 scale (courtesy of the Italian Ministry of the Environment). During 1998, each pond was sampled twice, using an inflatable boat, in late spring and in early autumn. This was to take into consideration seasonal variation that was indicated in a previous study of a subset of these ponds (Ruggiero et al., 2003). Maximum depth was measured with a graduated pole and the area of the pond surface covered by aquatic macrophytes visually assessed and given as an approximate percentage (%) to the nearest multiple of 10. On each sampling occasion a water sample and a measurement of conductivity and pH (WTW 340i Multiline probe) was taken from four randomly chosen locations at 10–20 cm below the water surface. The water samples were stored in a refrigerated box on site for transportation to the laboratory. Analysis of the samples included measurements of chlorophyll \( a \), nitrate, ammonium and phosphate following standard methods reported in APHA (1989) and Wetzel and Likens (1991). During sampling, the presence of frogs, newts and fish was recorded, without capture or identification. The odonate species presence was assessed from qualitative samples taken on both visits using a hand net with a 20 × 30-cm opening and a 0.25-mm mesh. All benthic habitats such as aquatic plants (helophytes and hydrophytes) and the un-vegetated sediments were sampled. These samples were fixed on site with 80% alcohol, and subsequently sorted and identified in the laboratory by hand. The odonate species determinations were made following the key of Carchini (Carchini, 1983) or by referring to material from Carchini’s collection. An odonate species was considered present if at least one larval individual was found in one of the two samples, while the presence of adults, even if recorded on site, was not considered in the analyses. Frogs, newts and fish were considered present if at least one individual was recorded. The larger depth measured in the two visits was taken as the maximum depth. The means of all other variables were considered in the following analyses, except location and forest percentage. Simple correlations between pairs of variables were made by the Spearman rank correlation test. Multiple regression analysis was performed in which the dependent (response) variable was the number of odonate species and the independent (predictor) variables were all the habitat characteristics. As many of these predictor variables may be dependent upon each other, the forward stepwise procedure was used, which includes at each step one new explanatory variable, specifically the one most associated with the response variable while being, at the same time, independent of the explanatory variables already included in the model. The criteria to include or exclude the variables from the regression model were: entry criterion \( F > 4.0 \), remove criterion \( F < 3.9 \). The number of species and all the habitat variables (except those expressed as percentages or presence/absence) were log-transformed. For Canonical Correspondence Analysis (CCA) the first matrix was represented by the presence/absence of all odonate species, and the second matrix was the habitat variables. Again, the variables were log-transformed, with the exception of those expressed as percentages or presence/absence. CCA was done with The Vegan Package (available at http://www.r-project.org/), a contributed package for the R environment. RESULTS A total of 14 odonate species was identified overall but the number of species in each pond was generally much lower, with a mean value of 1.9 species per pond (SE = 0.32), rising to 2.6 species per pond (SE 0.29) excluding the ponds without Odonata. The distribution of the species among the ponds was highly skewed: out of 31 ponds, eight had no species and another eight had only one species. The largest number of species found in any one pond was six, this number occurring in only one pond. The most widespread species was Enallagma cyathigerum, which was present in 16 ponds (Table 1). Multiple regression analysis showed that the number of odonate species was positively related to macrophyte coverage and negatively affected by increasing ammonium concentration (Table 2). The remaining habitat variables were not considered by the regression model, although there were some significant correlations found between the variables included and those not included. For example, ammonium concentration was positively correlated with altitude and chlorophyll \( a \), while negatively correlated with depth and frog presence; macrophyte coverage was negatively correlated with planktonic chlorophyll \( a \) concentration and positively correlated with frog presence (Table 3). The first three axes of the CCA analysis explained 16%, 10% and 8% of cumulative variance, respectively, and the environmental variables were significantly constrained in the ordination of species and ponds (\( p = 0.03 \), after 1000 permutations under the full model). The presence of frogs, the percentage macrophyte cover, altitude, chlorophyll \( a \) and ammonium were correlated with the first two axes (\( p < 0.05 \), after 1000 permutations). The effect of nitrate, pH and conductivity was negligible, and therefore these variables were not considered in the CCA plot. The CCA ordination diagram, which shows the first two axes of the CCA (Figure 1), indicated that the habitat variables were divided into two groups. The first group ran along the negative part of the first axis and included the four variables related to the absence of the Odonata (chlorophyll \( a \), ammonium, altitude and phosphate). The second group occurred through the first and the second quadrant and included all the remaining environmental variables. Accordingly, all species points were within the first and second quadrant, except Orthetrum coerulescens which was in the fourth quadrant. Table 1. Ecosyst. 15: 000–000 (2005) DISCUSSION Species richness and habitat characteristics When the findings of this research were compared with a previous study of lowland ponds of central Italy (Carchini et al., 2003) it was found that, besides altitude, the two pond sets differed regarding the surrounding vegetation. The lowland ponds were almost all within oak woodland, and shrubs were abundant on the banks of the ponds. In contrast, in the vegetation surrounding the mountain ponds shrubs were absent, possibly as a result of intense trampling by the herds of cows and horses. A few mountain ponds were surrounded by trees, which were mainly beech, while the majority were surrounded only by rough pasture. Unfortunately, no chemical data were available for the lowland ponds, so a full comparison between the two pond sets was not possible. The mountain ponds had lower odonate species richness. The average number of species in each pond was 1.9 (SE 0.32), rising to 2.6 (SE 0.29) when the eight ponds without Odonata were excluded. This is considerably lower than the average of 7.9 (SE 1.64) species per pond found in the lowland ponds. Multiple regression analysis of both data sets showed that the habitat variables affecting odonate species number in the mountain ponds were different from those of the lowland ponds. In the lowland ponds, pond area, riparian vegetation and depth positively affected the species number, while in the mountain ponds the significant influential variables were macrophyte coverage (positively related) and NH\(_4\) concentration (negatively related). There was a contrast in the effect of pond area between the lowland and mountain ponds suggesting that space is not a limiting factor in the mountain ponds, contrary to the generally accepted relationship between space and species number (for a review see Houston (1994)). Another relevant result was that the presence of fish, newts or frogs was not associated with the number of odonate species. This result might be expected for frogs and newts, whose predation on Odonata is usually low, but not for fish, which are well known to affect odonate assemblages (Corbet, 1999, table A.5.3. p. 615). However, not all fish are entomophagous, and we do not have data on the identity or dietary characteristics of the fish species present in these ponds. Finally, the amount of forest surrounding the ponds had no significant effect on number of odonate species, differing from what was shown by Rith-Narajan (1998) and Sahlén (1999), i.e. ponds surrounded by old woodland had richer odonate fauna than those surrounded by recently logged land. The findings from multiple regression analysis were confirmed by, and further detailed insight was given by, CCA and correlation analysis. In addition to ammonium, increasing phosphorus and planktonic chlorophyll \(a\) concentration (all indices of decreasing water quality) and increasing altitude were correlated with the absence of dragonflies. Increasing macrophyte coverage was identified as having the largest positive effect on odonate presence. This is not surprising as Aeshnidae and Coenagrionidae insert their eggs into macrophytes, while their larvae, as well as those of some Libellulidae species also live on the immersed stems of aquatic macrophytes. It seems that altitude negatively affects odonate presence indirectly. In central Italy the altitudinal limits for the most common hydrophytes (*Eleocharis palustris*, *Potamogeton perfoliatus*, *P. pectinatus*, *Myriophyllum spicatum*) vary from 1500 to 1800 m whilst the limit of helophytes such as *Phragmites australis* and species of *Typha* is at about 2000 m (Pignatti, 1982). As a consequence, increasing altitude results in a decrease of macrophyte diversity which has been shown to be negatively related with odonate species number (Sahlén, 1999). However, this relationship was not observed in the lowland pond set (Carchini et al., 2003). Species assemblage and habitat characteristics In central Italy, among the recorded species, the distributions of *E. cyathigerum*, *Sympetrum flaveolum* and to a lesser extent *Lestes dryas* are restricted to mountain habitats (Carchini, 1983). Most of the remaining species have a large altitudinal range, with the exception of *Coenagrion scitulum* and *Cercion lindeni* recorded previously only for sites well below 1000 m (Carchini and Rota, 1986). Several species are described as wanderers, migrants or pioneers, such as Ischnura elegans, Aeshna cyanea, Anax imperator, Libellula depressa, Crocothemis erythraea, S. flaveolum, Sympetrum fonscolombii (Schmidt, 1978; Moore, 1991, Corbet, 1999, pp. 10, 569 and tables A.10.3 and A.10.7); three of these species, A. imperator, L. depressa and I. elegans, were widespread throughout the pond set. The results of the CCA showed that I. elegans, L. depressa, A. cyanea and C. scitulum were in the first quadrant, which was characterized by increasing macrophyte coverage and newt presence. S. flaveolum and L. dryas were also in the first quadrant but isolated from the other species present, possibly due to their well known preference for temporary waters. E. cyathigerum, Coenagrion puella, A. imperator, C. erythraea and Sympecma fusca were in the second quadrant, characterized by frog and fish presence and increasing depth. Cercion lindeni and S. fonscolombii had an intermediate position between the first and second quadrant, and O. coerulescens had an isolated position that implies a preference for conditions similar to those in which no Odonata were present. However, the short length of several environmental vectors and the concentration of several species near the centroid indicates that the influence of the environmental variables in determining the species assemblage was weak. Furthermore, according to the results of the multiple regression analysis on number of species, it seems that frogs and newts did not directly affect the odonate species, but only varied with them. It is known that newts, L. dryas and S. flaveolum can also colonize temporary waters. Previous studies on the linkage between habitat variables and odonate assemblages made by CCA analyses have shown contrasting results. As there is no agreement on which environmental variables should be considered, the comparison among different studies is not easy. Using CCA analyses, it appears that many environmental variables exert an influence on odonate assemblages. Aquatic vegetation (assessed in different ways) has almost always been identified as a factor affecting odonate assemblages, whilst other variables, such as bank vegetation, surrounding forest, shade, pH, etc. have only been shown to have an effect in some studies, but not in others (Bang, 2001; Carchini et al., 2003; Schindler et al., 2003). Furthermore, even when the same species are present in different studies (Garcia-Aviles et al., 1995; Carchini et al., 2003, this study), they tend to cluster together and yet they respond to environmental variables in quite different ways according to the local conditions. This wide variation in the response of Odonata to habitat characteristics is possibly due to phenotypic plasticity and/or genetic differentiation. Conservation considerations Most of the variables found here that negatively affect odonate assemblages are similar to the variables that characterize the turbid state in shallow lakes (as described by Scheffer (1998)): high concentrations of nutrients and chlorophyll a, and a scarcity of aquatic vegetation. The large concentration of ammonium in several ponds (Table 1) appears to be an indication of organic pollution associated with upland herding. As other pollution sources are absent, the ammonium and phosphorus are assumed to come from faecal fertilization from livestock. In previous studies on a subset of these mountain ponds an increase in livestock grazing around the ponds was associated with an increase in pond turbidity and a decrease in macrophyte coverage (Solimini et al., 2000). The authors found that these conditions significantly reduced the total number of taxa in the ponds. However, the transition between a clear and turbid state can be unstable. In a detailed 4-yr study of the biggest pond, Lago della Duchessa (DUC), a shift from turbid conditions with high chlorophyll a concentrations and reduced macrophyte coverage to a clear condition with low chlorophyll a concentrations and high macrophyte coverage was observed to occur twice between 1997 and 2000 (Ruggiero et al., 2004). Furthermore, due to the typical arid summer condition of the Mediterranean area, these ponds are subject to large water-level variations. The ponds considered in this study had mean depths of around 1.6 m, and 12 ponds had depths of less than 1 m. Consequently, several ponds could possibly dry up, resulting in a strong reduction or a possible extinction of the resident odonate population. Upon pond re-establishment it is probable that re-colonization would favour the presence of pioneer species. The drying up of ponds was also observed in the lowland pond set, and the adults of some species were observed moving from pond to pond at distances of up to 2.7 km for the Zygoptera, and 5.9 km (in one day) for the Anisoptera (Carchini et al., 2004). There are no previous data on the water level fluctuations in the studied ponds. However, a depth reduction from 3 m (spring) to 20 cm (summer) was observed in DUC and, according to the memories of a shepherd working in the area, several decades ago DUC dried up. In addition, in the summer of 1999 the ‘Aquilente piccolo’ (AQP) pond, which was also inhabited by fish, an indication of prior stability, had also dried up. In conclusion, the low number of species per pond, the weak linkage among habitat variables with species presence, and the high presence of pioneer species, could possibly be explained by the instability of the ponds. Recent changes to the way in which mountain pastures in central Italy are exploited have probably worsened the impact of livestock on the ponds. In the past, the mountain pastures were grazed by sheep watched over by shepherds; the consequent watering time was short. Now, for economic reasons, sheep have been replaced by cows and horses which are left free to roam and to remain at the ponds, increasing the amount of faeces and urine in and around the ponds. Furthermore, both cows and horses usually go into the water, causing resuspension of the sediments and damage to the macrophytes. To limit the damage to benthic communities, including the Odonata, it seems useful to control the access of livestock to the ponds. In the past, several ponds were fenced, probably for reasons of hygiene, and water was made available to livestock only in drinking troughs. This practice, now largely abandoned, appears to be the primary mitigation procedure to safeguard the biotic diversity of mountain ponds, including that of the Odonata and in particular E. cyathigerum, S. flaveolum and L. dryas, whose distribution (in peninsular Italy) is limited to the standing water of mountain areas. Multivariate chemometrical classification and assessment of Lake Tuendae: A Mojave desert aquatic environment housing the endangered Mojave Tui Chub Grady Hanrahan a,*, Siraj Gibani b, Kent Miller c a Department of Chemistry, California Lutheran University, Thousand Oaks, CA, 91360, USA b College of Medicine, Pennsylvania State University, Hershey, PA, 17033, USA c Department of Chemistry & Biochemistry, California State University, Los Angeles, CA, 90032, USA ARTICLE DATA Article history: Received 8 August 2007 Received in revised form 16 April 2008 Accepted 1 September 2008 Keywords: Lake Tuendae Cluster analysis Principal component analysis Water quality Chemometrics ABSTRACT Lake Tuendae is a shallow, alkaline, artificially constructed Mojave Desert aquatic environment housing the endangered Mojave Tui Chub (Gila bicolor mohavensis). Detailed physiological response studies have been reported on the Mojave Tui Chub but few on the physico-chemical state of Lake Tuendae, one of four key Mojave Desert habitats for this species. Two sampling campaigns (spring 2004 and 2005) were conducted with correlation analysis, cluster analysis (CA) and principal component analysis (PCA) of physico-chemical water column and surface sediment quality parameters performed. CA proved useful in displaying parameter similarity for initial interpretation. PCA proved to be a more reliable display model and permitted the reduction of 14 parameters for the water column to four principal components accounting for 71% of the total variability. For surface sediments, four principal components accounted for 81% of the total variability. This work highlights the successful use of chemometric multivariate techniques in helping elucidate the physico-chemical make-up of shallow desert aquatic environments, and instructive for investigators assessing the health of aquatic species in such habitats. 1. Introduction Shallow lake and pond environments typically exhibit highly stochastic temporal dynamics in physico-chemical parameters due primarily to hydrodynamic considerations (Vareschi, 1982; Çelik and Ongun, 2007; Odour and Schagerl, 2007). These systems are further characterized by such qualities as low total nitrogen (TN) to total phosphorus (TP) ratios, low stratification, high primary productivity and substantial internal transport of sediments by resuspension and sedimentation (Vareschi, 1982; Lijklema, 1994; Talling, 2001; Settacharnwit et al., 2003; Thorbergsdóttir and Gíslason, 2004). The management of such systems is often problematic as shallow systems respond quickly to physical changes in their environments. Such changes may be dramatic (e.g. eutrophication) and result in noticeable changes in community structure (Kallio, 1994; Koehler et al., 2005; Spears et al., 2007). The importance of assessing the status of such environments is thus evident and provides an avenue to help maintain species diversity and richness. The Mojave Tui Chub (Gila bicolor mohavensis), for example, is a fish species known to exist only in four aquatic locations in the Mojave Desert region of the southwestern United States. These populations are listed as endangered by the State of California and the US Department of the Interior, US Fish and Wildlife Service. Detailed abiotic response studies have been reported for this species (Castleberry and Cech, 1986; McClanahan et al., 1986), but few on the physico-chemical state of their aquatic habitats. Full multivariate analysis and characterization of physico-chemical parameters in such systems would thus prove meaningful. Being able to distinguish between natural and anthropogenic sources of pollution in such systems is vital for interpretation purposes and for effective management practices. Various modelling and multivariate techniques have been effectively employed to describe water quality conditions, correlations between parameters/sites and pollution sources including hydrodynamic modelling (Hamilton and Schladow, 1997; Bonnet and Wessen, 2001; Naithani et al., 2007), cluster analysis (CA) (Singh et al., 2005; Markovic et al., 2006; Boyacioglu and Boyacioglu, 2007; Kannel et al., 2007), correlation analysis (Shuhaimi-Othman et al., 2007), discriminant analysis (DA) (Santos-Roman et al., 2003; Kannel et al., 2007) and principal component analysis (PCA) (Simeonov et al., 2000; Petersen et al., 2001; Micó et al., 2006; Rao et al., 2006). Such techniques provide meaningful data reduction and normalization, and aid in isolating specific interactions, correlations and groupings in complex environmental datasets. This work presents a detailed evaluation of physico-chemical water and surface sediment quality parameters in one key Mojave Desert aquatic habitat, Lake Tuendae, using correlation analysis, CA, and PCA. Lake Tuendae is a shallow, alkaline, artificially constructed aquatic environment located in an area of harsh environmental conditions. Two spring sampling campaigns (2004 and 2005) were conducted with 14 water column and 10 surface sediment parameters examined to assess water quality relationships and potential sources of pollution. Results characterize Lake Tuendae according to its physico-chemical parameters and possible interactions between the two compartments, thus providing valuable information for assessing the health of the Mojave Tui Chub and other species present. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study site Lake Tuendae (35°08′N latitude; 116°06′W longitude, elevation=237 m) is a shallow, artificially constructed aquatic habitat (<1 ha) located in the 414 km² Soda Lake Basin of the Mojave Desert, Southern California, USA, and houses the endangered Mojave Tui Chub (G. bicolor mohavensis). Two distinct aquifer systems influence the region: a carbonate rock-based system in the Soda Mountains and the Mojave River Sink recharged from percolation through Afton Canyon and Kelso Wash. A Lake Tuendae connection to Soda Springs is established through seepage. A mean annual precipitation level (concentrated between November and March) of 4in. has been reported for the Soda Lake basin (US Department of the Interior, 1999). Air temperatures in the Mojave Desert region can undergo seasonal extremes (−6.7° to 40.6 °C) (Archbold, 1996). Lake Tuendae is recharged from a well through a fountain in the center of the lake with average water levels ranging from 0.94m in the east portion to depths of 1.7m in the western section (Archbold, 1996). Lake Tuendae has limited protection from evaporation and is reported to sustain an annual evaporative loss of about 410,000 ft³ (Mojave National Preserve, 2003). It is known to gradually fill with sediments and cattails with the last known dredging activity occurring in 2001. Human influences are pronounced on the southern (site A) and eastern portions (site B) as they are within 10m of the Zzyzx Desert Studies Center. 2.2. Sample collection and storage Four sampling sites were chosen for both water column and surface sediments: site A (pier — 1.2 m depth), site B (eastern — 0.85 m depth), site C (northern — 1.0 m depth) and

Depth measurements reported are 2004 values and agree with those taken during the 2005 campaign and other reported studies (Archbold, 1996). For the 2004 study, 10 water column and four surface sediment samples were collected for each site. All sampling equipment and reagent and storage bottles were first washed with 10% (v/v) HCL, rinsed with ultrapure water (18.2mΩ, Nanopure Diamond, Barnstead, USA), air dried and stored in Ziploc bags until sampling. Water column samples were taken half the distance between the sediment and water surface at each site using a long handled HDPE dipper (Global Water Instrumentation, Inc., USA). Samples (including duplicates and field blanks) were placed into 125 mL HDPE bottles and stored at 4 °C until analysis (within 48h). Surface sediments were collected at a three inch depth using a decontaminated Teflon scoop (Fisher Scientific, USA). Excess water was retained to prevent the loss of fine particle material associated with the bottom of the surface water body. Samples were placed in 250 mL HDPE bottles and stored at 4 °C until digestion (within 48 h). 2.3. Reagents and standard solutions All reagents were of analytical grade and prepared in ultrapure water unless otherwise stated. Stock standard solutions (1000 mg L−1) for TN and TP analyses were prepared from potassium nitrate (Fisher Scientific, USA) and potassium dihydrogen phosphate (Fisher Scientific, USA), respectively. Working standards were prepared by appropriate dilutions for calibration purposes. Metal working standard solutions were prepared from diluting 1000 mg L−1 stock solutions (in 1% HNO3, Spex CertiPrep, Inc., USA). Appropriate blanks and certified lake water (ION-20, National Water Research Institute, CA) and lake sediment (LKSD-1, National Research Council, CA) reference materials were incorporated to ensure good analytical quality. 2.4. Physico-chemical analyses Fourteen water column parameters (Table 1a) and 10 surface sediment parameters (Table 1b) were analyzed for all sites. Dissolved oxygen (DO), temperature and pH were measured directly on site at the time of sampling by an Orion 4-Star Portable pH/DO meter (Thermo Scientific, USA). Conductivity and total dissolved solids (TDS) were measured on site with a WTW conductivity/TDS field meter (3300i, Geotech, USA). Total nitrogen (TN) and TP were measured by US EPA methods 351.2 and 365.4, respectively, using a modified automated flow injection (FI) analyzer (Model 3500, FIA Lab Instruments, USA). Metals were analyzed via an on-line preconcentration flow injection-flame atomic absorption (FI-AAS) method described by Tony et al. (1999). Here, the FI analyzer (with incorporation of a microcolumn packed with C18 material) discussed above was connected to an atomic absorption spectrophotometer (Model 6701, Shimadzu, JP) for routine analyses. For sediments, US EPA method 3050B was employed for sediment digestion prior to metal analysis. For TN and TP analysis, Lachat methods 10-107-04-1-C and 10-115-01-1-E, respectively, were employed on dried sediment samples using persulfate oxidation digestion. The organic matter content was determined by APHA standard method 209F. Routine calibrations were performed and certified reference materials incorporated. 2.5. Multivariate analysis Multivariate chemometric analysis on whole (all sites) water column and surface sediment data was performed using JMP 7.0 software (SAS Institute, Inc.). Only the 2004 multivariate worked data is reported due to completeness of the dataset and for brevity purposes. Descriptive statistics for 2005, however, are reported. A correlation matrix was first generated to assess similarities between parameters in both the water column and surface sediments. CA using Ward’s Method after parameter standardization was then employed to help identity the number and characteristics of groups within both compartments. PCA with Varimax rotation was then used to transform a number of (potentially) correlated parameters into smaller, orthogonal principal components (PCs). Data characteristics Tables 1a and b provide 2004–2005 descriptive statistics of whole physico-chemical Lake Tuendae water column and surface sediment data, respectively. Mean parameters for both years were analyzed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (p>0.05). With the exception of TP and TDS, parameters in the water column exhibited a normal distribution. For surface sediments, all parameters except TP, TN and OM showed normal distributions. TP concentrations (2004) ranged from 0.03 mg L$^{-1}$ in site C to 0.17 mg L$^{-1}$ in site B with an overall mean for all sites of 0.09±0.01 mg L$^{-1}$. High temporal and spatial variability of TP in shallow environments, especially those <1ha such as the one studied, has previously been shown (Branco et al., 2005; Søndergaard et al., 2005). Though not considered eutrophic (TP=0.26 mg L$^{-1}$), a low TN:TP ratio (11:1) for Lake Tuendae suggests possible risk of bloom-forming cyanobacteria (Xie et al., 2003). No studies were performed during the sampling campaigns to confirm the presence of cyanobacteria. The TP rich sediments shown in this study (whole data mean=0.72±0.12 mg L$^{-1}$, 2004) may serve as an important source of the supply in the water column. Such a process could be the result of internal transport and possible outburst of Microcystis blooms (Lijklema, 1994; Xie et al., 2003). Site B sediments had the highest mean (n=4) levels at 0.82±0.06 mg L$^{-1}$. There is no external river or stream inflows that could carry suspended particles to account for the relatively high TDS concentration in the water column. This occurrence could be explained by the strong evaporative processes coupled with wind influences with subsequent increases in soluble parameters. As shown, most of the Fe input into Lake Tuendae accumulates in the surface sediments (whole data mean=7879±162.2 $\mu$g g$^{-1}$) likely via coagulation and settling processes. Elevated Mn levels (whole data mean=724±47.1 $\mu$g g$^{-1}$) in the sediments could suggest that manganese is included in stable iron sulfides such as pyrite (Toshiyuki and Yasushi, 1982). Higher OM levels in sediments have been shown to suggest an important retention of heavy metals (Micó et al., 2006). 3.2. Correlation coefficients of $r \geq 0.40$ were taken as meaningful at 99% confidence (Tokalioğlu and Kartal, 2002) and are highlighted in bold. For the water column, a strong negative correlation (−0.75) was observed between DO and water temperature. Conductivity showed correlations with Pb (0.85), TDS (0.69), Cu (0.64) and to a lesser extend with Cd (0.43). TDS also showed correlation with Zn (0.40), Cd (0.42), Fe (0.57), Cu (0.59) and Pb (0.70). Moderate correlations between OM and the heavy metals were shown in the correlation analysis (Section 3.2). TN and TP relationships in sediments have been well established (Noges et al., 1998; Koehler et al., 2005; Trevisan and Forsberg, 2007). The TP sediment pool, for example, is composed of a number of operationally-defined phosphorus (P) components (e.g. dissolved and particulate, organic and inorganic.) each with their own release pathway affected by equilibrium conditions between the surface sediment and the overlaying water (Lijklema, 1994; Amini and McKelvie, 2004; Spears et al., 2007). Moreover, fluctuations in TP have been explained by variations in total Fe and dissolution of carbonate associated phosphate (Knöscke, 2005). 3.4. Principal component analysis Clustering does not imply dependency only similarity. There is, typically, no cause and effect relationship among the clusters of the data points. Therefore, PCA after Varimax rotation was performed to gain a more reliable display method and greater understanding about the relationships within the two datasets. Varimax searches for an orthogonal rotation (i.e. a linear combination) of the original factors such that the variance of the loadings is maximized (Kaiser, 1958). As shown in Table 4a, the cumulative contribution of the first four PCs accounted for 71% of the cumulative variance in the whole water column dataset. These four were retained and used for Varimax rotation. The corresponding Scree plot (Fig. 3a) shows the sorted eigenvalues as a function of the eigenvalue index. As shown in Table 4b, PC 1 had higher loadings for conductivity, TDS, Cd, Cu and Pb and may represent metal accumulation with particulate matter. PC 2 is associated with Ni. PC 3 represents the carrier of micronutrients as higher loadings for TN, TP, Fe and Mn were shown. PC 4 is associated with DO and Zn. PCA rendered an important data reduction into four principal components describing 71% and 81% of the cumulative variance for whole data water column and surface sediments, respectively. PCA revealed that Lake Tuendae water column data consisted of three major components representing a carrier of micronutrients (TN, TP, Fe and Mn), metal accumulation with dissolved particulate matter and one associated with DO and Zn. A fourth represented Ni alone. For sediments, a major component associated with OM, TN, TP, Fe, Mn, Ni, Pb and Zn may represent nutrient and heavy metal accumulation in the sediments. Additionally, a component consisting of Fe and Mn justifies our suggestion of Mn being included in stable iron sulfides. Though no noticeable anthropogenic inputs (e.g. sewage) were observed, we acknowledge that the human inhabited Desert Studies Center is a potential source of nutrients and metals, especially when considering the higher loading sampling sites A and B (those nearest to the Desert Studies Center). Overall, however, the Desert Studies Center is a controlled location primarily used for research efforts with a limited number of visitors per year. High evaporative desert processes are believed to play a major role in water quality dynamics. Despite the potential for disturbances, Lake Tuendae is currently considered a safe refuge for the Mojave Tui Chub. Concerns are apparent, though, due to the introduction of the exotic mosquito fish (Gambusia affinis), which may consume eggs and larvae of endemic fish (Mojave National Preserve, 2003). Efforts to monitor the effect of this exotic species, as well as lake turbidity, on the status of the Chub are ongoing. In summary, multivariate chemometric techniques proved useful in examining and interpreting whole water column and surface sediment data in Lake Tuendae. It proved highly significant in our understanding of the physico-chemical make-up of shallow, desert aquatic environments and will likely be instructive for investigators assessing the health of species in such environments. It must be noted, however, that alternative multivariate clustering techniques would prove valuable in such studies. The use of self organizing maps (SOM), a type of unsupervised artificial neural network (ANN), can complement PCA by producing low dimensional (one or two-dimensional) representations (maps). They are used to expose underlying relationships in a given environmental dataset and are arguably becoming the technique of choice for many investigators due to their robustness as a computational tool. Being able to distinguish between natural and anthropogenic sources of pollution in such systems is vital for interpretation purposes and for effective management practices. Various modelling and multivariate techniques have been effectively employed to describe water quality conditions, correlations between parameters/sites and pollution sources including hydrodynamic modelling (Hamilton and Schladow, 1997; Bonnet and Wessen, 2001; Naithani et al., 2007), cluster analysis (CA) (Singh et al., 2005; Markovic et al., 2006; Boyacioglu and Boyacioglu, 2007; Kannel et al., 2007), correlation analysis (Shuhaimi-Othman et al., 2007), discriminant analysis (DA) (Santos-Roman et al., 2003; Kannel et al., 2007) and principal component analysis (PCA) (Simeonov et al., 2000; Petersen et al., 2001; Micó et al., 2006; Rao et al., 2006). Such techniques provide meaningful data reduction and normalization, and aid in isolating specific interactions, correlations and groupings in complex environmental datasets. This work presents a detailed evaluation of physico-chemical water and surface sediment quality parameters in one key Mojave Desert aquatic habitat, Lake Tuendae, using correlation analysis, CA, and PCA. Lake Tuendae is a shallow, alkaline, artificially constructed aquatic environment located in an area of harsh environmental conditions. Two spring sampling campaigns (2004 and 2005) were conducted with 14 water column and 10 surface sediment parameters examined to assess water quality relationships and potential sources of pollution. Results characterize Lake Tuendae according to its physico-chemical parameters and possible interactions between the two compartments, thus providing valuable information for assessing the health of the Mojave Tui Chub and other species present. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study site Lake Tuendae (35°08′N latitude; 116°06′W longitude, elevation=237 m) is a shallow, artificially constructed aquatic habitat (<1 ha) located in the 414 km² Soda Lake Basin of the Mojave Desert, Southern California, USA, and houses the endangered Mojave Tui Chub (G. bicolor mohavensis). Two distinct aquifer systems influence the region: a carbonate rock-based system in the Soda Mountains and the Mojave River Sink recharged from percolation through Afton Canyon and Kelso Wash. A Lake Tuendae connection to Soda Springs is established through seepage. A mean annual precipitation level (concentrated between November and March) of 4in. has been reported for the Soda Lake basin (US Department of the Interior, 1999). Air temperatures in the Mojave Desert region can undergo seasonal extremes (−6.7° to 40.6 °C) (Archbold, 1996). Lake Tuendae is recharged from a well through a fountain in the center of the lake with average water levels ranging from 0.94m in the east portion to depths of 1.7m in the western section (Archbold, 1996). Lake Tuendae has limited protection from evaporation and is reported to sustain an annual evaporative loss of about 410,000 ft³ (Mojave National Preserve, 2003). It is known to gradually fill with sediments and cattails with the last known dredging activity occurring in 2001. Human influences are pronounced on the southern (site A) and eastern portions (site B) as they are within 10m of the Zzyzx Desert Studies Center. 2.2.
