As described by our sediment core data (Fig. 5) and an observed increase in July chlorophyll \( a \) (1997 = 21.3 \( \mu \)g/L; 1998 = 177.8 \( \mu \)g/L), Org Lake crossed the clear–turbid threshold into an unstable transitional lake in 1998. In fall 1998, Zimmer et al. (2001) eradicated the fathead minnow population using fish toxicants, resulting in the lake being fishless again in 1999. Our sediment core DCA axis 1 trend shows a slight reversal during the early 2000s shortly after the fish population was eliminated. By 2005, fathead minnows had once again re-colonized the lake and, as shown in the sediment core data, the lake is currently in a turbid state (Fig. 5). The four clear lakes (Grandokken, Blakesely, Skunk, and Pisa) show no evidence in the sediment core records that they have crossed the clear–turbid threshold, which confirms a regime of stable clear states that likely has persisted over the last ~150 yr (and longer in Grandokken and Skunk, which were analyzed beyond the \( ^{210}\mathrm{Pb} \) record). The three turbid lakes (Leverson, Mavis West, and Frolund) were found to have crossed the clear–turbid threshold in ~1915, 1957, and 1985, respectively (Fig. 5). We see no evidence that these lakes have ever returned to a regime with stable clear states. Frolund Lake was bio-manipulated in 2001 by introducing walleye (Sander vitreus, a piscivore) to control the fathead minnow population (Potthoff et al. 2008). The sediment record clearly shows this had a minor impact on the diatom communities (Fig. 5) but was an insufficient intervention to transition the lake back to a stable regime of a clear state. Fathead minnow were found to recolonize the lake soon after the introduction of walleye. The lakes that are classified as transitional based on the contemporary limnology have been observed in either clear or turbid state during July sampling (Morrison, Org, Mavis East, and Bellevue). This category of lakes differs slightly with the observations from our sediment records. Morrison Lake appears to have been historically very close to the clear–turbid threshold. Observations and bio-manipulations of Morrison Lake from 1996–2002 and 2010–2011 document a history of fluctuations in the fish populations but limited success in maintaining a clear-water macrophyte-dominated state (Zimmer et al. 2002, Potthoff et al. 2008). Given the sediment record for Morrison, these observations may typify the lake’s history over the last ~150 yr as being in a transitional state. Org, Bellevue, and Mavis East lakes have crossed the clear–turbid threshold within the last ~20 yr (Fig. 5). We have previously discussed how the contemporary and paleo-limnological data describe the ecological shifts in Org Lake. Similar to other lakes, Bellevue and Mavis East have undergone biomanipulations using walleye introductions (Potthoff et al. 2008). While walleye stocking appeared to have a cascading effect leading to temporary clear-water ecological conditions, lake condition did not return to the pre-disturbance regime. This finding is similar to our observations from Lake Christina where biomanipulations and induced clear-water states have failed to persist (Hobbs et al. 2012). In effect, the lakes that exhibit these short-term shifts in contemporary limnology are in an unstable regime (sensu Bayley and Prather 2003), which leads to a classification of transitional. In reality, these lakes may have reached a stable turbid state as described by their long-term legacy of recently crossing the clear–turbid threshold. It is often assumed that prior to European settlement, lakes in this region existed in a regime of a stable clear-water state. Our findings confirm this; all lakes including several with sediment records dated back over 1,000 years were in a stable clear state before European settlement. The impacts of gradual, regional land-use changes and nutrient inputs to lakes are known to have altered the ecology of many lakes in Minnesota (Ramstack et al. 2003, 2004). This is also in line with what has been found in European lakes (Davidson et al. 2005, Sayer et al. 2010c, Randsalu-Wendrup et al. 2014). A large paleolimnological database of European lakes synthesizing information on over 1,800 studies found only a few cases of a perturbation prior to about 1850 (Battarbee et al. 2011). We were able to confidently use fossil diatom assemblages to define the historical clear-water regimes in our shallow lake dataset. The timing of the regime shifts was not consistent among the lakes. This highlights the watershed-specific factors that influence shallow lake ecology, similar to the recent findings of Maheaux et al. (2016). We posit that it is the regime history of the aquatic ecosystem that defines or provides the context for the modern ecological state (clear or turbid) of the lake. Four of our lakes were historically clear (ca. 1850) and remain clear today, with no indication in the sediment record that they have undergone any perturbations (Fig. 5). Seven of our lakes were historically clear, but are now in a regime with unstable transitional or stable turbid states. The questions are why are only some lakes driven over the stability threshold and can we prevent others from crossing this threshold? Drivers of ecosystem change Previous work on shallow lakes in the PPR has highlighted the impact that hydrologic changes and increasing benthivorous and planktivorous fish can have on the food web of a shallow lake (Zimmer et al. 2001, Hanson et al. 2012), similar to other regions (Jeppesen et al. 2000, McGowan et al. 2005, Bayley et al. 2007, Cobbaert et al. 2014). We also find evidence from limnological monitoring that nutrients (or bottom-up effects) can play a role in regime shifts (Zimmer et al. 2009; sensu Scheffer and Carpenter 2003, Cobbaert et al. 2015). While top-down effects, coupled with increased nutrient inputs over time, appear to be the main reason for perturbations in the modern ecology of shallow lakes, is the same true for the long-term regime shifts in the lakes throughout this region? Based on comparison between our modern training set and core trajectories of diatom turnover, total phosphorus does not appear to be the predominant driver of the regime shifts in this suite of lakes (Fig. 6; Appendix S1: Fig. S12). We also tested whether there is a relationship between the TP optima for each diatom species and its position within the benthic-planktonic continuum or DCA axis 1 and did not find one (\( r = 0.019; P = 0.33 \)). Furthermore, the diagnostic statistics for the DI-TP (\( \lambda_R / \lambda_P \) scores) suggest that the assemblages are not responding to TP; the lakes that have gone through a regime shift have low \( \lambda_R / \lambda_P \) scores (Table 3). It does appear that diatom communities are reasonable indicators of nutrient changes in stable clear lakes (\( \lambda_R / \lambda_P \) scores are high in these lakes; some show an increase, some show a decrease). In Blakesley Lake, for example, the diatom communities track changes in the water column TP over time (Fig. 6). While the TP in Blakesley Lake increases through time, the lake does not undergo a regime shift in spite of nutrient enrichments (Hobbs et al. 2014). Furthermore, the estimated concentrations of DI-TP in this lake (range of 55–85 \( \mu \)g/L) were in the meso- to eutrophic range and hover around the threshold of 62 \( \mu \)g/L TP that Zimmer et al. (2009) estimated between clear and turbid lakes. The long-term stability of Blakesley Lake has been attributed mainly to stable trophic interactions due to the lack of hydrologic connectivity preventing colonization by fish (Hobbs et al. 2014). In general, the stable clear lakes we studied have nutrient concentrations that would promote a turbid, phytoplankton-dominated state were the lakes to undergo a major food-web perturbation. Many of the lakes in this region are impacted by planktivorous fish (e.g., fathead minnow *Pimephales promelas*, bluegill *Lepomis macrochirus*, and small yellow perch *Perca flavescens*) and benthivores (e.g., bullhead *Ameirus* spp, and white sucker *Catostomus commersonii*). Surveys of fish communities in these lakes indicate that stable clear lakes were fishless or had lower fish biomass than turbid lakes (Table 1). This suggests that fish have at least some impact on long-term ecological regime characteristics of shallow lakes. Work on shallow lakes in Europe has produced similar findings on the drivers of algal and ecological change (Van Geest et al. 2003, McGowan et al. 2005, Søndergaard et al. 2005, Sayer et al. 2010a). From sediment records in two shallow Danish lakes, McGowan et al. (2005) reported that total phosphorus alone was not a significant explanatory driver of regime shifts; it was only significant in combination with changes in planktivorous fish and macrophyte abundance. Similarly, a large spatial survey of Danish lakes showed that smaller lakes (<1 ha) had lower fish biomass and greater macrophyte coverage (Søndergaard et al. 2005). In the UK, Sayer et al. (2010a) showed that diatom-inferred TP did a poor job of explaining long-term ecological changes in macrophyte communities. In the Netherlands, Van Geest et al. (2003) showed a greater likelihood of clear-water condition when benthivore biomass was low and the lake area was small. In addition to top-down food web effects, changes in water level may also be an important driver of ecosystem change in these lakes. Some of our study lakes underwent a regime shift in the late 1980s (Frolund, Mavis East, Bellevue), which was a time when a drought ended in the PPR resulting in higher water levels in many lakes (Hanson et al. 2005), and presumably more movement and introduction of fish. In addition to facilitating fish introductions, increased water level has also been shown to lead to a loss of macrophytes (Wallsten and Forsgren 1989), which could further promote a turbid state. Recent research in northern Alberta, Canada, has highlighted how precipitation and water-level fluctuations can induce inter-annual state shifts, however the authors suggest that subsequent change in nutrients is the ultimate driver of ecological change (Cobbaert et al. 2014, 2015). It is possible that the persistence of macrophytes could create a positive feedback loop, in which high plant abundance causes more severe anoxic conditions in the winter as the plants decay, helping to keep fish biomass low (Meding and Jackson 2003). If this were the case, then rising water levels leading to a decrease in macrophyte biomass would also promote rising fish populations. In addition, many of the stable clear lakes have macrophyte communities that contain *Chara* spp., which can form dense mats and act as a nutrient sink through incorporation into plant biomass and co-precipitation of phosphorous with calcite (Kufel and Kufel 2002). In the UK, Sayer et al. (2010b) have documented two macrophyte communities associated with shallow lakes; communities that are stable and communities considered to be crossing the clear–turbid threshold or crashing. The UK stable clear lakes are dominated by *Chara* spp. and *Ceratophyllum* spp., which are the same dominant plant communities in our group of stable clear lakes. Macrophyte communities dominated by *Potamogeton* spp. appear more susceptible to regime shifts (Sayer et al. 2010b). The difference between the UK lakes and PPR lakes is that nutrients are implicated as the main driver of a crashing or shifting macrophyte community in the UK lakes, whereas our results suggest that nutrients are not the primary driver. *Ecological legacies and management implications* Human activities, in particular land-use histories, have long been recognized as important for understanding and conserving both terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems (Foster et al. 2003). Historical activities create ecological legacies and reduced resiliency for shallow lakes, thus effects of natural perturbations and human activities in modern landscapes may be accentuated (or buffered in the case of lake rehabilitation) by events in previous decades or even centuries. We believe knowledge of ecological legacies of shallow lakes is fundamental to management for at least two reasons. First, interpreting present lake features is only possible in light of earlier conditions and lake responses to historical influences. Second, shallow lake rehabilitation strategies can only be effective when managers allow for limitations imposed by ecological legacies, and we think this is especially true for lakes within highly altered landscapes. Ecological legacies in shallow lakes often include effects of large perturbations from single stressors, result from impacts incurred over time, or reflect cumulative effects of multiple stressors. Resulting transitions often establish modern characteristics and ecological stability of these waters (Hobbs et al. 2012). Ecological legacies in shallow lakes have been described as hysteresis in the context of short-term alternative equilibria (Scheffer et al. 1993, Beisner et al. 2003). However, data shown here indicate that ecological legacies of shallow lakes often predispose these waters to perpetually unstable conditions and predominantly turbid water. In fact, long-term reversal of persistent turbid conditions has generally eluded shallow lake managers. The reality for many of these lakes is that they are now part of a managed landscape and will likely require repeated management interventions (i.e., biomanipulations) to maintain (or frequently induce) desired clear-water states. We believe knowledge of ecological legacies provides a context for interpreting results of shallow lake responses and should improve future management decisions. Patterns shown here also offer insights that should help classify clear and turbid lakes and assess their potential for rehabilitation. For example, several lakes we studied (Org, Mavis East, and Bellevue Lakes) showed stable turbid-lake characteristics, but diatom communities indicated that these lakes remained close to the critical transition thresholds, perhaps showing these would be good candidates for management to reestablish or sustain clear states. Diatom communities indicated that other lakes had moved farther across the transition threshold (e.g., Leverson, Mavis West, and Frolund Lakes), and these would likely prove difficult to rehabilitate. Indeed, Mavis East was biomanipulated in 2001 by reducing planktivorous fish biomass by two consecutive years of walleye fry stocking (Potthoff et al. 2008). A clear water state was observed during 2002–2004, but when the lake was revisited in 2007 it had reverted back to a turbid state (K. Zimmer, unpublished data). Responses of Mavis East show how lake management can induce periods of clear water without achieving transitions to a stable clear state (i.e., crossing back over the threshold had not been achieved). Following walleye stocking and biomanipulation, Frolund Lake developed even stronger water-quality improvements than Mavis East, but again the reduction in fish biomass was insufficient to induce a transition to a stable clear-water state. Considering both modern characteristics and paleolimnology of PPR shallow lakes will help managers understand how historical legacies, perturbations, and regime shifts set the stage for the prevailing ecological conditions of shallow lakes in modern landscapes. We think lake managers should be better able to predict whether a shallow lake will be responsive to biomanipulations and rehabilitation efforts by considering patterns in long-term diatom assemblage turnover such as those shown here. Notes: Values for turbidity, chlorophyll a, total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), Daphnia, and macrophytes are median values of data collected mid-summer (July) from 1996 to 2011. Macrophyte totals were calculated by the number of times a plant was collected on a rake tow, summed across all plant species. Fish data represent the biomass of planktivores and benthivores, presented as median values (with range) of data collected from 2009 to 2011. Turbidity was measured in nephelometric turbidity units (NTU). modified from Deppe and Lathrop (1992), where a weighted plant rake was tossed for 3 m along the lake bottom in two directions at 15 locations in each lake. The summed total number of submerged macrophyte species collected on the 30 throws was used as an index of overall abundance of submerged macrophytes. Fish communities were sampled with three mini-fyke nets deployed perpendicular to shore and one experimental gill net set along the deepest contour in each lake for 24 h. The total biomass of planktivorous and benthivorous fish captured in the four nets was used as an index of fish biomass. Daphnia were sampled with an integrated column sampler (Swanson 1978) at five locations in each lake. Results were averaged across the five samples and expressed as Daphnia/L. Samples for chlorophyll a, total nitrogen (TN), and total phosphorus (TP) were collected at three locations in each lake, with the mean value across the three samples used for analysis. Chlorophyll a was determined with acetone extraction followed by fluorometric analysis. Total phosphorus was estimated with persulfate oxidation followed by ascorbic acid colorimetry, while total nitrogen was analyzed with persulfate oxidation and second derivative spectrophotometry. Finally, turbidity was measured using a nephelometer. Sediment coring and dating Sediment cores were recovered from canoes, using a piston-type corer (Wright 1991), in the summers of 2009–2011. Cores were sub-sampled at a resolution of 0.5–1.0 cm, freeze dried, and prepared for diatom and radioisotopic analysis.
